answer.rationale: With only 14 days before the primary contract lapses and the line running at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, an outright switch to an unproven-at-scale low-cost vendor (c2) risks delivery disruption that outweighs its cost benefit, especially since c2's record only confirms quick onboarding and accurate invoicing, not sustained reliability at full committed volume. Memory c4 indicates that benchmarking the incumbent against market/competitor quotes during renewal negotiations previously recovered real margin and improved payment terms without any transition risk, and c1 confirms incumbent renewals preserve integration stability and delivery continuity. Given the mandate is an 18% cost cut with no increase in delivery risk, the best single move this cycle is to use the low-cost vendor's quote as negotiating leverage with the incumbent rather than switching outright or deferring past the contract's hard expiration. I verified c4 and c2 because the plan's validity hinges on whether negotiation historically closed enough of the cost gap (c4) and whether the low-cost quote is a credible, well-founded benchmark (c2) rather than an artifact of different scope or terms. Second-sourcing (c3) and deferral (c5) are not viable this cycle given the hard 14-day deadline and lack of committed capacity buffer.
